Why India has introduced semiconductor programmes

Semiconductors are important for telecommunications, computing, defence, transport, industrial automation, renewable-energy equipment and consumer electronics. Dependence on imported components can expose these sectors to international supply disruptions. Developing domestic capabilities can improve supply-chain resilience, create skilled employment and increase the value added within India's electronics industry.

A successful semiconductor ecosystem requires more than constructing fabrication plants. It also needs chip designers, testing facilities, manufacturing equipment, materials suppliers, technical training institutions and reliable infrastructure.

India Semiconductor Mission

India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) is an independent business division within the Digital India Corporation (DIC), functioning under the national semiconductor policy framework led by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Its role includes facilitating the development and implementation of India's semiconductor and display manufacturing and design ecosystem.

The Union Cabinet approved the Semicon India Programme on 15 December 2021, with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore. The programme provided support for semiconductor manufacturing, display manufacturing and chip design.

The principal support categories under the original programme

  • Semiconductor fabs: Support for manufacturing facilities that fabricate semiconductor devices on wafers.
  • Display fabs: Support for facilities that manufacture electronic displays.
  • Compound semiconductor and related facilities: Support covering compound semiconductors, silicon photonics, sensors and semiconductor ATMP or OSAT activities.
  • Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme: Support for eligible domestic semiconductor design activities, including design infrastructure and incentives.

The Design Linked Incentive Scheme addresses the design stage. It should not be confused with a programme that only finances the construction of wafer-fabrication plants.

Semicon 2.0

On 15 July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0 with a total outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore. This expanded the policy emphasis towards developing a more complete domestic semiconductor ecosystem.

Its 6 pillars are:

  1. Chip design.
  2. Semiconductor machines and materials.
  3. Additional semiconductor fabrication facilities.
  4. Advanced packaging and further ATMP or OSAT development.
  5. Research and development.
  6. Talent development.

The inclusion of materials, equipment and workforce development reflects a basic industrial requirement: a fab cannot operate effectively without suitable inputs, technicians and supporting services.

Chips to Startup and skill development

The Chips to Startup (C2S) programme, launched by MeitY in 2022, supports semiconductor design skills and academic participation. Its original capacity-building target was 85,000 industry-ready people in specialised semiconductor design fields.

The ChipIN Centre at C-DAC supports access to chip-design tools and related services. This helps students, researchers and eligible startup teams participate in design activities without each institution independently purchasing all the necessary tools.

Gujarat Semiconductor Policy, 2022–27

Gujarat notified the Gujarat Semiconductor Policy (2022–27) to encourage semiconductor and display projects within the state. The policy addresses infrastructure, land, utilities, approvals and fiscal assistance for eligible investments.

A particularly important provision is the additional state capital assistance for eligible projects approved by ISM. Under the policy, the state assistance is calculated at 40% of the capital-expenditure assistance provided by the Government of India, subject to the applicable eligibility conditions.

Do not confuse the bases of calculation. The Gujarat policy's 40% additional assistance is linked to the eligible central capital assistance. It is not an unconditional grant equal to 40% of a project's total investment cost.

Dholera Semicon City

The Gujarat policy identifies Dholera Special Investment Region (Dholera SIR) as a location for developing a semiconductor ecosystem. Its proposed supporting facilities include Industry 4.0-enabled common infrastructure, Internet of Things-based warehousing, marking and packaging facilities, and testing laboratories.

These are policy provisions and development intentions. A planned common facility should not be described as already operational solely because it appears in the policy. The policy also provides for eligible incentives at locations elsewhere in Gujarat, subject to its conditions.

Gujarat projects: location, activity and reported status

The following distinctions are based on official project and production updates available for 2026. They distinguish commercial packaging or testing operations from a wafer fab that is still being developed.

ProjectLocationActivity and reported status
MicronSanand, GujaratSemiconductor assembly and testing; commercial production commenced in February 2026.
Kaynes SemiconSanand, GujaratOSAT manufacturing; commercial production commenced in March 2026.
CG SemiSanand, GujaratOSAT facility; commercial production commenced in July 2026.
Suchi SemiconSurat, GujaratSemiconductor packaging; commercial production line inaugurated in September 2026.
Tata Electronics semiconductor fabDholera, GujaratWafer-fabrication project under construction as reported in September 2026; not reported as commercially operational at that time.

The Tata Electronics wafer-fabrication project at Dholera is fundamentally different from the listed commercial packaging and testing operations. The July 2026 Union Cabinet release identified 2028 as the expected commissioning period for India's first commercial semiconductor fab under the programme. This was a planned future milestone, not an achieved commissioning date.

According to the Press Information Bureau release dated 19 September 2026, the Semicon 1.0 programme had 12 approved semiconductor projects, of which 5 commercial semiconductor units had become operational. The 5 comprised Micron, Kaynes, CG Semi, Suchi Semicon and CDIL Semiconductor at Mohali. This count describes the status reported on 19 September 2026, not a guarantee that the same count remained unchanged thereafter.

Prelims focus

  • ISM operates as an independent business division within Digital India Corporation.
  • Semicon India Programme: approved on 15 December 2021 with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore.
  • Semicon 2.0: approved on 15 July 2026 with an outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore and 6 pillars.
  • Gujarat Semiconductor Policy covers 2022–27 and identifies Dholera SIR for semiconductor ecosystem development.
  • Gujarat's additional capital assistance is linked to 40% of eligible central capital assistance.
  • Trap: Commercial ATMP or OSAT production at Sanand or Surat does not mean the Dholera wafer fab has begun commercial production.

[Press Information Bureau, Indian Semiconductor Mission, 3 February 2023, organisational structure and objectives; Press Information Bureau, India Semiconductor Mission, 23 March 2022, original programme and outlay; Press Information Bureau, Cabinet Approves Semicon 2.0, 15 July 2026, budget and 6 pillars; Press Information Bureau, Government Adopts Multi-Pronged Roadmap to Build a Robust Semiconductor Talent Pipeline, 30 July 2026; Government of Gujarat, Department of Science and Technology, Gujarat Semiconductor Policy (2022–27), Sections 4.1 and 4.2.1; Press Information Bureau, SEMICON India 2026 Concludes Successfully, 19 September 2026; Press Information Bureau, SEMICON India 2026 inauguration release, 17 September 2026, plant statuses; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: India Semiconductor Mission, National Programmes and Gujarat's Semiconductor Ecosystem

body:
Meaning of a cyber-physical system

A conventional computer processes information in electronic form. A physical machine acts on the real world by moving materials, applying force, generating heat or performing other physical operations. A cyber-physical system (CPS) combines computation and communication with the monitoring or control of physical processes.

The word cyber refers here to computing and communication, while physical refers to machinery, equipment or other real processes. A cyber-physical system uses information from physical conditions to support suitable decisions or actions.

Essential components

  • Sensors: Detect physical conditions such as temperature, pressure, position or vibration.
  • Controller or computer: Processes measurements and determines an appropriate response according to its programmed logic.
  • Actuators: Convert control instructions into physical action, such as adjusting a valve or changing motor speed.
  • Communication: Transfers information between components when they are separated or interconnected.
  • Feedback: Provides updated measurements so the system can evaluate the effect of its actions.

How a feedback-based industrial system works

Consider a factory conveyor driven by an electric motor. A sensor measures the motor's temperature. The controller compares this measurement with permitted operating conditions. If the temperature becomes excessive, the controller may slow the motor or stop the conveyor. A fresh temperature reading indicates whether the action has improved the condition.

This is a feedback loop: the physical process affects the sensor measurements, the controller interprets the measurements, and an actuator changes the physical process. The updated physical condition can then be measured again.

Such systems appear in industrial machinery, automatic temperature control, vehicle safety systems, electricity networks and modern transport equipment. They may function through local controllers, connected networks or a combination of both.

The meaning of Industry 4.0

Industry 4.0 refers to the greater integration of digital technologies, connected equipment, data and intelligent automation within industrial production. Cyber-physical systems are among its central foundations.

The term Fourth Industrial Revolution reflects the broad sequence of changes in industrial production.

StagePrincipal developmentIndustrial change
Industry 1.0Water power and steam power.Mechanisation of production.
Industry 2.0Electric power and assembly-line production.Large-scale mass production.
Industry 3.0Electronics, computers and programmable control.Greater automation of machines.
Industry 4.0Connected cyber-physical systems, data and smart automation.More integrated and responsive production.

The stages describe major technological shifts, not exact dates at which every factory changed. Industries may still use technologies from several stages at the same time.

Automation, the Internet of Things and CPS

Automation means operating a process with reduced need for continuous direct human intervention. A machine following a fixed programmed sequence is automated, but it may not exchange information with other machines or adapt to changing conditions.

The Internet of Things (IoT) refers to physical objects equipped with sensors, software and connectivity that allow data to be collected and exchanged. In industrial settings, connected sensors and machines are often described as the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT).

IoT and CPS frequently work together, but they emphasise different aspects. IoT emphasises connectivity and information exchange. CPS emphasises the integration of computation with physical processes, commonly including monitoring, feedback and control.

Internet connectivity is not compulsory for every CPS. A local computer controlling a machine through sensors and actuators can also perform cyber-physical functions. Conversely, a connected sensor that only sends measurements is not necessarily controlling a physical process.

A connected production line

Suppose several machines report their operating conditions to a common monitoring system. If one machine slows down, the system can alert an operator or adjust other equipment where suitable control arrangements exist. This can help reduce unnecessary stoppages. The benefit depends on reliable measurements, communication and properly designed operating rules.

Why Industry 4.0 extends beyond robotics

Robots can form part of an Industry 4.0 factory, but installing robots alone does not establish a fully connected production system. Industry 4.0 involves the broader coordination of sensors, machines, software, information and workers.

A production facility may combine robotic equipment with digital quality inspection, condition monitoring, inventory information and computer-assisted production scheduling. The purpose is to use information from different activities to improve industrial decisions.

Prelims focus

  • CPS integrates computation with physical processes through sensing and control.
  • Sensors measure conditions; actuators produce physical action.
  • Feedback allows a controller to respond to the effects of earlier actions.
  • Industry 3.0 emphasises computer-based automation; Industry 4.0 adds stronger connectivity and cyber-physical integration.
  • IoT emphasises connected objects and information exchange.
  • Trap: Not every automated machine requires the Internet, and not every connected sensor independently controls machinery.

[Ministry of Heavy Industries, SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0, Industry 4.0 and cyber-physical systems overview; NIST, Digital Manufacturing: Requirements and Challenges for Implementing Digital Surrogates, abstract, 12 December 2018; World Economic Forum, What Is the Fourth Industrial Revolution?, overview of industrial transitions; Ministry of Heavy Industries, SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0, Smart Manufacturing Demo and Development Cell section; online sources consulted 5 November 2026.]
